questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: To explore a European country, and experience a daily life in another culture.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I think it was pretty easy. There was a lot of paper works and deadlines to remember. But I think that both University of Cologne and Erasmus team at KU were very helpful and sent all information, and answered questions fast.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The incomings team at the university arranged a lot of both practical and academic introduction events. And also, there were events of more social character to get to know the city and the other exchange students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: The university adviced us to start searching very early, so I began as soon as I knew I was going. At first I found it a bit difficult, since I didn't know how high expectations I could have, and also didn't hear anything back from the first many people I contacted. However I ended up finding a really nice room.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
I recommend to make a 'profile' on
wg.de
(they have a nice app), where you can upload information about your self, so that people can reach out to you. Once I did this, I got multiple offers. However I do recommend to start early, since it is difficult to find nice housing in the city, and many end up living 30-60 minutes out of town.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The incomings team were very helpful in sending everything you need. However it does need a lot of time to both fulfill all the deadlines, and get everything done. Everything could be done online, which was very nice, and different from what I have heard about many other universities in Germany.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could always contact the incomings team, both online or in person.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Start in good time, have patience and pay attention to hard deadlines. They are not very flexible if you miss them.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: One of my courses 'Capitalist societies and climate change' was one of the best courses I have had during my studies. However, I had different experiences in other courses. I think the structure can seem a bit 'outdated' from a danish perspective, fx. calling professors by their title and last name. Furthermore, sit-in exams (one our) is the most common type - even on a master level - which I personally found a bit wierd, especially in social science courses. So prepare yourself to write a lot in hand. Of course there are also courses with portfolio or essay exams. You can check up on this before signing up. Another good thing to know is, that you don't have to go to the exam in the courses you sign up for, so you can actually sign up for more courses than you need, and then do a 'trial week'. I didn't know this until after the course registration period, but I think it is a very nice way to get a feeling of the professor and the course. I would highly recommend to do this.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took more courses in sociology, than political science (which is what I study at home). Generally I think the level was okay, not too hard and not too easy. The assigned readings are however much less than what i'm used to at home, which I found super nice. It gives more space to actually dive into the assigned texts, and of course also more free time.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I took lectures and seminars. Both pretty similar to forelæsning and holdundervisning in UCPH. However the seminar courses were very small, which could be a bit intense.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Democratic Theory and Practice
- Diversity, Cohesion and Conflicts in Societies and Organisations - Social Inequality in Education
- Contemporary Societies: Social Structure and Social Change
- Analysis of Social Change - Capitalist societies and climate change

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
All three courses except "Diversity, Cohesion and Conflicts in Societies and Organisations - Social Inequality in Education". The professor in this course seemed unprepared for the class sessions, and I personally did not like the format of teaching he provided. 

The three others were very interesting and different from each other - and courses I know from home. I would however recommend to take seminars, if you - like me - tend to get a bit unfocused during a lecture. Especially the course 'capitalist societies and climate change' with Philipp Golka was very nice, and he managed to create a very inclusive room in providing a good discussion.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: You pay a pretty high semester contribution before going. However this covers 'free' transportation all over Germany (not ICE trains).

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Housing more expensive. 
Food/groceries not more expensive, but similar to danish prices I would say. 
Not much cheaper to go out to eat, but drinks are cheaper.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't attend any of them, but I know there are a lot of options available.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are a lot of activities such as sports offered by the University. Also Erasmus Cologne makes activities from city trips to nights out. I attended some of these in the beginning of my stay. It is a great way to get to know people. However I preferred to arrange things on my own with the people I got closer to. Also I had friends visiting from Denmark many of the weekends, which was a priority I had from the start. But definitely go to some of the events in the beginning, it is fun even though it can seem a bit wierd in the start.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Explore the city, its many different areas, and just enjoy living in another city, without the many 'obligations' you maybe usually have at home.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go on day trips/weekend trips, Cologne connects so many places in europe by train, fx. Paris (4 hours aprox), Bruxelles, Amsterdam. 
If you are there during the winter, go to the christmas markets - also the ones in the center. Unlike the Danish ones, they are quite cute and very well-visited, so preferably weekdays are better than during the weekend.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy, very similar in many ways. However people are simply just very nice in this city, and I think that is really worth appreciating.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I lived with a german girl, and I believe looking for housing with locals is the best way to get to know locals. I also did get to know some of the students from my courses, however more on a superficial level. Be open and go to events and stuff, if you want to socialize with the local students. However, I believe it is kind of similar to students at UCPH, that it is difficult for exchange students to actually 'get under the skin' of the locals.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I didn't find it very much different than Denmark. However there are of course some smaller differences such as paying cash, closed supermarkets on sundays an so on, but not particularly challenging ones, you just have to remember to bring cash and do your groceries on saturdays. What I found challenging was however the pretty high amount of homeless and very ill people in the streets. I found it hard to see people at the bottom of society receiving no help.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openminded and friendly people. I think it maybe has to do with Cologne being a very multicultural and 'smaller' city, compared to fx. Berlin. I think people care less about being and lookin cool, and more on spending time with good friends and family. I really enjoyed the many Turkish restaurants and food experiences, and in general the more multicultural society, especially in Ehrenfeld, where I also found accomodation.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Choose courses you find interesting, and wouldnt be able to choose at home. 
2) If possible, find housing in a nice area. Do some research on areas you might find nice (I lived in Ehrenfeld, a very nice 'nørrebro-ish' area). It makes it much easier to do things close to your house. 
3) Enjoy your time, be openminded to learn new things, even though Germany is similar to Denmark. I found it nice that it was not a huge culture chok, but rather, that I could enjoy the smaller and bigger differences between the cultures.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure to double check when your classes are taking place. Some might even be on saturdays.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Experiences a different kind of daily life, enjoying time by myself more and get to know people from all over the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Knowing how much you should study and memorize for a one hour written sit-in exam.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
